summary: The article examines how quantum computing threatens current encryption such as RSA and ECC while also enabling new defenses like post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution. It cites researchers, industry figures and bodies including NIST and CNSS, and stresses preparing now by moving to quantum-resistant algorithms. It frames the field as an arms race between computational advances and security.
one_line: Quantum computing endangers RSA and ECC encryption but also enables post-quantum cryptography and QKD, so organizations must prepare for "Q-Day" now.
key_facts: Quantum computers use qubits, which can represent a 0, a 1, or any quantum superposition of these states, unlike classical bits.

Dr. Sarah Langston of the University of New Arcadia said quantum computers could reach processing power "orders of magnitude greater than the most powerful supercomputers of today"; she was interviewed on October 10, 2023.
Present-day encryption algorithms like RSA and ECC rely on the difficulty of factoring large prime numbers or solving discrete logarithm problems, which quantum computers might render trivial.

Michael Anderson of FlexCyber Inc. warned at the Quantum-Safe Security Conference on September 5, 2023 that "What would take a traditional computer millennia to crack could be done by a quantum computer in hours or even minutes."
"Q-Day" is the hypothetical point when quantum computers become powerful enough to break widely-used cryptographic algorithms.
Post-quantum cryptography aims to build algorithms that remain intractable for both classical and quantum computers.

Dr. Rajesh Singh and his team at the International Cybersecurity Center of Excellence work on lattice-based encryption; their paper dated November 17, 2023 proposes an approach hard for quantum computers to break.
NIST in the United States has been running a competition since 2024 to standardize post-quantum cryptographic algorithms.
Quantum key distribution (QKD) exploits the fact that observing a quantum system alters its state, so eavesdropping is immediately noticeable.
Quantum Secure Inc. has begun deploying QKD alongside existing infrastructure; CEO Elizabeth Mortensen said in a December 1, 2023 webinar that QKD could "usher in an age of unbreakable encryption."
The Committee on National Security Systems (CNSS) advisory says classified information that must be protected for more than 10 years should be encrypted with quantum-resistant algorithms by 2025.
Laura Gibson, head of cyber-risk management at GlobalTech Enterprises, said the company is "mindful of the potential backdoors that could be exposed" as it adds quantum-computing applications.
Upgrading existing systems to quantum-resistant algorithms comes with its own challenges and costs.
